speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Government is prepared for the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to continue making net losses over the next one to two years should the tightening of monetary policy be maintained; and (b) whether and, if so, how will Government funding be affected by MAS’ financial position.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether MAS’ $7.4 billion loss will have any impact on the Government budget; (b) if so, what is the impact; and (c) whether any reconsideration is needed on how MAS contributions in the Government budget is to be used given the volatility in its returns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) whether he can clarify the context for the loss of $7.4 billion reported by MAS in their financial statement for FY2021/2022; and (b) whether the recorded loss will have implications on the Government’s strong Singapore dollar policy and overall budget position for the current financial year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The negative currency translation effect is not relevant to MAS’ investment performance, which is measured in foreign currencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It also has no bearing on the international purchasing power of the OFR, or on MAS’ conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As MAS tightened monetary policy in October 2021 and January 2022, the Singapore dollar had strengthened against several of the foreign currencies in which the OFR are held.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This meant a currency translation loss when the OFR were reported in Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The negative currency translation effect has no implication for the international purchasing power of the OFR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, given the purpose of the OFR in safeguarding the international purchasing power of the Singapore dollar, it is the foreign currency value rather than the Singapore dollar value of the OFR that matters.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS’ net loss in Singapore dollar terms also has no implications for its conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The aim of MAS' monetary policy is to secure low and stable inflation as the basis for sustained growth over the medium term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS, as Members know, conducts an exchange rate-centred monetary policy, managing the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When inflationary pressures build up, as they have over the past year, MAS allows the trade-weighted exchange rate to appreciate faster.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Negative currency translation effects do not have any bearing on MAS’ ability to manage the exchange rate; rather they are a consequence of MAS’ conduct of exchange rate policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me, in my capacity as the Minister for Finance, answer the questions relating to the impact of MAS’ net loss on the Government’s Budget position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the outset, let me clarify that MAS’ overarching mandate is to ensure macroeconomic stability.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government does not expect MAS to deviate from this mandate in order to maximise its contributions to the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS contributes to the Government’s Budget in two ways.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, under the Net Investment Returns (NIR) framework, the Government can spend up to 50% of the expected long-term real return on the net assets invested by MAS, GIC, and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The NIR framework is designed to provide a steady, sustainable stream of income to help meet the Government’s expenditure needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The NIR is based on the long-term expected returns of the three investment entities and therefore, is not affected by their short-term performance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, similar to other Statutory Boards, MAS makes contributions to the Government in lieu of corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is based on 17% of the net profit for the year after offsetting cumulative losses from previous financial years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the case of MAS, the Government recognises that its contributions will vary considerably from year to year due to the combined effect of currency translation and investment returns on MAS’ balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The smoothening formula has helped to mitigate the impact of MAS' net loss on the Government’s Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Investment returns are inherently volatile reflecting market conditions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government has taken steps to ensure that this volatility does not unduly affect the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is neither responsible nor prudent for us to rely on windfall surpluses in any given year to fund our increased structural spending needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also thank the Deputy Prime Minister for the comprehensive reply.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How much has MAS contributed to Government's consolidated funds in the past five years, beyond FY2021/2022 that was reported in the press?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How does MAS decide how much money MAS needs to contribute to the consolidated fund every year?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are all based on a formula and MAS will publish every year in its annual report the contributions it makes to the consolidated fund based on these formulas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that for the investment returns, we do have the NIRC framework where it smoothens out over a long period of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We call it the long-term expected real returns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister, why are these investment returns from OFR, and hence, the foreign exchange translation effects and fluctuations, not counted under the NIRC framework where the returns are smoothened out over the long period of time, through that methodology?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second question, in MAS' annual report, it also mentioned the higher interest rate expenses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask if the rising interest rates will add to the overall interest expenses of the Government, given the size of securities the Government intends to issue going forward?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The NIR framework covers our investments by MAS, Temasek and GIC – three investment entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The investments are largely in foreign currencies, they are in foreign assets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they will be converted, translated into Singapore dollars, into a net asset base, which is smoothened out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The smoothening formula for the net asset base computation, in a way, helps to moderate foreign currency effects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in fact, MAS' contributions through the NIR mechanism to NIRC is very much incorporated already into the present NIR framework.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second question of the impact of interest rates on interest expenses, that is something that will happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With rising interest rates, there will be implications for MAS' interest expense.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it also has an implication for MAS' investment income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, taking both into consideration, over the longer-term, MAS should be able to manage the effects of rising interest rates on its financials.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While MAS had chalked up a $7.4 billion loss in 2022, both the investment companies Temasek Holdings and GIC have chalked up hundreds of billions of dollars of additional profits because of the good markets in 2021 and 2022.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask the Minister, overall, are we expecting a further increase in our foreign reserves in 2023?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am not sure where Mr Leong Mun Wai got "hundreds of billions of dollars" in returns, but the performance by Temasek and GIC have been published, we can find out what they are.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is what matters for budgetary matters.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we work out next year's Budget in 2023, Members will see what is the NIR contribution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This framework has been worked out, I think it is something that is sound and it is something that we will continue to manage prudently and responsibly.
